question: Can the spectral normalization used by idealized Muon/Shampoo updates produce better early-stopped minority and class-balanced generalization than Euclidean gradient descent by learning weak and dominant data components at equal rates?

key_findings.claim: Under exact joint diagonalizability, zero initialization, population squared loss, and a linear model, the paper derives decoupled trajectories in which gradient flow learns component c at rate s_xx,c whereas spectral gradient flow moves every active singular component at unit rate until its component-specific target is reached.
key_findings.evidence: Condition 1 jointly diagonalizes Sigma_yx and Sigma_xx. Equation (2) gives the exponential GD trajectory, while Proposition 1 and its continuous-time form give the piecewise-linear spectral trajectory. Lemma 3.1 verifies the condition for orthogonal equal-norm Gaussian class means with isotropic noise, where component strength is tied to class prior.

anchors.section: Appendix B.2, gradient-flow and spectral-gradient-flow limits

key_findings.claim: The exact discrete-time SpecGD trajectory in Proposition 1 is false for a generic fixed step size: without clipping the final step, an active scalar component overshoots its optimum and then oscillates rather than becoming exactly equal to s_yx,c/s_xx,c.
key_findings.evidence: The update derived in Appendix B.2 adds eta while w_c*s_xx,c<s_yx,c. If alpha_c=s_yx,c/s_xx,c is not an integer multiple of eta, the next update crosses alpha_c; the gradient changes sign and the normalized step reverses, producing a two-point oscillation. The displayed formula instead replaces the iterate by alpha_c after the crossing even though no clipping or adaptive terminal step is defined. The restriction eta<min_c alpha_c does not imply divisibility. The continuous-time SpecGF formula remains valid, but claims that fixed-step SpecGD converges to the same solution do not follow.

anchors.section: Appendix B.2, discrete SpecGD update and claimed closed form
Appendix C, claim that all fixed-step optimizers converge to one solution

key_findings.claim: For the paper's Gaussian-mixture population model, continuous-time SpecGF has an early interval on which its minority-class and class-balanced loss are provably below those of both ordinary and normalized gradient flow by gaps at least linear in time.
key_findings.evidence: Simplified Theorems 1 and 2 give lower bounds of order mu*t through the time at which SpecGF first fits the minority component. The full Theorems 3 and 4 prove these bounds under explicit restrictions on the minority prior, signal-to-noise ratio, number of classes, majority-minority gap, zero initialization, and equal-norm orthogonal means.

anchors.section: Appendix B.3, full Theorem 3 and class-loss Eq. (7)
Appendix B.3-B.4, balanced-loss proof and full Theorem 4

key_findings.claim: Those theorems establish a favorable transient only in a specially aligned population model, not a generalization guarantee for practical Muon on finite, nonlinear, cross-entropy problems.
key_findings.evidence: The proof needs exact population joint diagonalizability and identifies minority classes with weak eigendirections only because class means are orthogonal, equal norm, and corrupted by isotropic Gaussian noise. The experiments instead use cross-entropy, random initialization, finite samples, nonlinear networks, momentum, approximate Newton-Schulz updates, and hybrid treatment of vector parameters. The authors explicitly leave finite-sample and cross-entropy theory open.

anchors.section: Appendix C-D, relaxed-condition check and practical optimizer implementations
Appendix F, limitations and open questions

key_findings.claim: In balanced deep linear factorizations, the paper predicts that depth changes each SpecGD saturation time from a first power to an L-th-root dependence and therefore shrinks the relative majority-minority saturation gap.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 2 handles the bilinear case and Section 3.3 gives Delta T=(ratio)^(1/L)-1. Proposition 4 proves the corresponding diagonal trajectory for L>=2 under balanced infinitesimal initialization and k=d. A two- versus four-layer Colored-MNIST plot is offered as an empirical parallel, including a similar speedup for NGD for which no matching theorem is given.

anchors.section: Section 3.3, deep-linear saturation-gap formula and Figure 6
Appendix B.5, full bilinear proposition and proof

key_findings.claim: Synthetic finite-sample tests broadly reproduce the population trajectory, but only near the constructed model: one 2,000-sample perturbation has joint-diagonalization residual about 0.013 and Muon follows SpecGD qualitatively.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 10-13 compare population and finite-sample trajectories, random initialization, momentum Muon, and one relaxed matrix B. They report qualitative curve agreement rather than a sweep over alignment error, sample size, dimension, conditioning, or statistical uncertainty.

anchors.section: Appendix C, Figures 12-13 and relaxed Condition 1

key_findings.claim: Across several from-scratch imbalanced benchmarks, Muon usually improves early minority or worst-group performance relative to Frobenius- and max-norm momentum methods and often relative to SGD.
key_findings.evidence: Colored-MNIST uses a 99% digit-color correlation; CIFAR-10/100 uses 20:1 step imbalance; Dominoes uses a 95% MNIST-CIFAR spurious correlation; and the appendices add heavy-tailed Barcoded MNIST. At CIFAR-10 epoch 1 and imbalance 20, the paper reports roughly 20% minority accuracy for Muon versus below 10% for NMD and Signum. Most other results are curves without tabulated endpoints or uncertainty.

key_findings.claim: The paper contains substantial negative evidence against a blanket Muon-generalization claim: Adam matches or beats Muon in several settings, and spectral preconditioning itself does not always beat elementwise preconditioning.
key_findings.evidence: Adam is better than Muon on MultiNLI, comparable on CelebA and the TinyStories/add-k mixture, and best for minority accuracy when fine-tuning an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet on imbalanced CIFAR-10. On Colored-MNIST, the authors report no discernible Shampoo-Adam or vShampoo-RMSProp gap. Their discussion explicitly says Adam is sometimes better, and loss-reweighted NMD beats ordinary-loss Muon very early.

anchors.section: Appendix D.2.2, pretrained CIFAR negative result

key_findings.claim: The practical optimizer comparisons do not isolate spectral normalization because Muon sends vector parameters to Adam and Shampoo uses SGD or Adam grafting, while the tested Muon uses only one Newton-Schulz iteration.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix D states that vector parameters use Adam by default under Muon, Shampoo updates are rescaled by SGD/Adam grafts, and Muon performs a single Newton-Schulz iteration. Consequently, observed differences cannot be attributed uniquely to the exact UV^T update analyzed in the theory.

key_findings.claim: Several model-selection choices can inflate the empirical advantage: some CIFAR/Colored-MNIST hyperparameters appear selected by reported test minority/group-balanced accuracy, compute is not matched, and the deliberately large batches are known to enlarge adaptive-versus-SGD gaps.
key_findings.evidence: Colored-MNIST and CIFAR sweep figures are labeled with test accuracy, and the text selects the best final group-balanced or minority accuracy without identifying a validation split. Muon, Signum, NMD, and Adam use different learning-rate scales and momentum values; R=20 hyperparameters are reused at all imbalance ratios. Appendix D explicitly chooses large batches because prior work finds a larger Adam-SGD gap there. No wall-clock or FLOP-matched early-stopping comparison is supplied.

anchors.section: Appendix D.2.1, reuse of R=20 settings

key_findings.claim: The language-model evidence is exploratory rather than a validation of the principal-component theorem.
key_findings.evidence: TinyStories uses only 500 training stories and 50 validation stories, a 2,000-token vocabulary, and different weight decay for Muon (zero) versus SGD/Adam (1e-4). The main text calls the held-out results test performance whereas the appendix calls them validation performance and uses validation loss for hyperparameter selection. Rare/frequent token accuracy is not a measurement of data-moment principal components, and context-dependent token difficulty is uncontrolled.

anchors.section: Appendix D.5, TinyStories protocol and Figure 26

key_findings.claim: The nonlinear spectral diagnostic changes the theoretical construct from data principal components to singular values of a training-logit matrix, so low singular-value KL divergence is supporting analogy rather than a test of the stated mechanism.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix D.10 normalizes singular values of the k-by-n logit matrix and compares them with a uniform vector. SpecGD/Muon has lower KL divergence on one-hidden-layer Gaussian and CIFAR-10 models, but no link is proved between these logit singular vectors and the Sigma_xx/Sigma_yx basis used by the theory.

anchors.section: Appendix D.10, nonlinear spectral metric and Figure 31

key_findings.claim: There are smaller internal notation defects in the proof record, but they do not by themselves overturn the continuous-time bounds.
key_findings.evidence: Equation (7) reuses c as both the focal class and the summation index where j is intended. Equation (17) defines a class-balanced gap as an unnormalized sum even though the following derivative and the original definition use 1/k. The discrete/continuous distinction is also blurred when empirical fixed-step methods are said to converge exactly according to the continuous trajectory.

method.core_idea: Replace practical matrix optimizers by spectral steepest descent, diagonalize a population linear regression problem, and use class imbalance to turn equal-rate singular-component learning into an early-stopping generalization advantage.
method.mechanism: For a gradient U Sigma V^T, SpecGD takes the normalized matrix step U V^T. Under a shared singular basis for input and input-output moments, Euclidean gradient flow approaches each optimum exponentially at a rate set by the corresponding input eigenvalue, whereas spectral gradient flow advances every unsaturated singular coordinate at unit speed. Orthogonal Gaussian class means make majority classes the large moment components and minority classes the weak ones. Deep balanced factorizations replace target amplitudes by their L-th roots, reducing saturation-time disparities. Experiments treat Muon and Shampoo as approximate practical realizations of this balancing effect.
assumptions: The formal loss is population mean-squared error for a linear predictor, with zero initialization for the principal theorems.
Sigma_yx and Sigma_xx are exactly jointly diagonalizable; the canonical data model enforces this with orthogonal equal-norm class means and isotropic Gaussian noise.
Class priors are sufficiently imbalanced relative to signal-to-noise ratio, class count, and mean norm to satisfy the theorem-specific inequalities.
The strongest loss-gap statements concern continuous-time gradient flow only and stop at the first minority-component saturation time.
Deep-linear results use balanced, aligned, infinitesimal initialization; Proposition 4 additionally assumes k=d.
Practical Muon is assumed to retain the relevant behavior despite momentum, approximate Newton-Schulz orthogonalization, stochastic finite batches, cross-entropy, and nonlinear architectures.
For group imbalance, spurious/core features are assumed to coincide with dominant/weak spectral components.
For next-token prediction, token-frequency groups and logit singular values are treated as analogues of the class-prior components without a formal correspondence.
Early epoch/iteration comparisons are treated as meaningful despite unmatched optimizer computation and occasionally test-guided hyperparameter selection.

techniques.role: Uses the polar factor U V^T as the exact normalized steepest-descent direction under the matrix spectral norm.
Reduces population matrix dynamics to independent scalar singular-coordinate trajectories.
Constructs an orthogonal Gaussian mixture whose moment eigenvalues directly encode majority and minority priors.
Differentiates minority and class-balanced loss gaps to prove early SpecGF advantages over GF and normalized GF.
Derives layerwise diagonal SpecGD dynamics and an L-th-root shrinkage of component saturation disparities.
Perturbs exact joint diagonalization and compares empirical finite-sample/Muon paths with population SpecGD predictions.
Tests whether optimizer gains are concentrated on rare classes, rare tokens, or groups that oppose a spurious correlation.
Uses KL divergence between normalized logit singular values and a uniform spectrum as a nonlinear balanced-learning proxy.

evaluations.setting: Twenty-class, 100-sample, d=200 heavy-tailed Gaussian-mixture classification with a linear model and cross-entropy.
evaluations.metric: Class-balanced and worst-class test accuracy over training.
evaluations.result: Early-stopped SpecGD is reported above NGD and SignGD at any displayed stopping point; training-loss curves were made comparable using optimizer-specific learning rates.
evaluations.baseline: NGD and SignGD; this is finite-sample cross-entropy rather than the theorem's population squared-loss setting.

evaluations.setting: Colored-MNIST with 99% digit-color correlation, full-batch four-layer MLP, 500 epochs, five runs.
evaluations.metric: Majority- and minority-group test accuracy trajectories.
evaluations.result: Muon/SpecGD improve minority accuracy much earlier than Frobenius- and max-norm counterparts, but Shampoo does not visibly beat Adam and vShampoo does not visibly beat RMSProp.
evaluations.baseline: NGD, SignGD, SpecGD, NMD, Signum, Muon, RMSProp, vShampoo, Adam, and Shampoo.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-10/100 with 20:1 step imbalance, ResNet-18/50, batch 2,048, 200 epochs.
evaluations.metric: Minority- and majority-class test accuracy over epochs.
evaluations.result: Muon is best in the displayed from-scratch curves; on CIFAR-10 at epoch 1 and R=20 it is about 20% minority accuracy versus below 10% for NMD/Signum. With ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18, Adam instead gives the best minority accuracy.
evaluations.baseline: NMD, Signum, Adam, and Muon with optimizer-specific selected hyperparameters.

evaluations.setting: MNIST-CIFAR Dominoes, ResNet-34, 95% spurious MNIST-label correlation, three runs.
evaluations.metric: Worst-group accuracy and decoded worst-group accuracy after retraining a linear head on balanced validation features.
evaluations.result: Muon is above SGD throughout; its early gain over Adam disappears later, while Muon, Shampoo, and Adam all have much higher decoded accuracy than SGD.
evaluations.baseline: SGD, Adam, Shampoo, and Muon selected by validation worst-group accuracy.

evaluations.setting: MultiNLI with BERT and CelebA with ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50, four and five runs respectively.
evaluations.metric: Average and worst-group test accuracy under validation-selected fine-tuning budgets/hyperparameters.
evaluations.result: Muon/Shampoo beat SGD in worst-group accuracy; Adam is better on MultiNLI and comparable on CelebA.
evaluations.baseline: SGD, Adam, Shampoo, and Muon with extensive validation sweeps.

evaluations.setting: TinyStories subset with 500 training and 50 validation stories, four-layer Transformer, 100 epochs.
evaluations.metric: Validation loss and top-1/top-5 accuracy for tokens below the 50th versus above the 80th training-frequency percentile.
evaluations.result: Muon converges faster and narrows the frequent-rare gap relative to SGD and Adam in the displayed curves.
evaluations.baseline: SGD and Adam; Muon has zero weight decay while both baselines use 1e-4.

evaluations.setting: A 90/10 mixture of 18,000 TinyStories sequences and 2,000 add-k sequences, 200 epochs.
evaluations.metric: TinyStories top-1/top-5 and add-k exact-match accuracy.
evaluations.result: Muon learns the majority and minority domains more evenly than SGD but performs comparably to Adam.

evaluations.setting: One-hidden-layer Gaussian model and imbalanced CIFAR-10 nonlinear networks under cross-entropy.
evaluations.metric: KL divergence from a uniform normalized singular-value vector for the training-logit matrix.
evaluations.result: SpecGD/Muon maintain lower KL divergence than Frobenius/max-norm variants in the reported plots.
evaluations.baseline: NGD and SignGD for the Gaussian MLP; NMD and Signum for CIFAR-10.

limitations: [Author-stated] Formal results are restricted to population squared loss; finite-sample generalization and cross-entropy are open.
[Author-stated] Exact joint diagonalizability is central and may fail outside the constructed Gaussian mixture; sequential language data lacks an identified analogue of the moment components.

[Reviewer-identified] Proposition 1's fixed-step SpecGD closed form silently clips the last component step. Generic constant normalized steps overshoot and oscillate, invalidating the claimed exact discrete convergence.

[Reviewer-identified] Orthogonal equal-norm means, isotropic noise, zero/aligned initialization, strict prior inequalities, and early stopping make the theorem much narrower than the empirical narrative.
[Reviewer-identified] Practical Muon and Shampoo are hybrid/grafted approximate algorithms, so experiments do not isolate the exact spectral step used in the theory.

[Reviewer-identified] Several key results tune using what is labeled test accuracy or do not identify a validation split; most outcomes are plots without numerical tables, intervals, or significance tests.
[Reviewer-identified] Large batches were deliberately chosen because they enlarge adaptive-optimizer gaps, and no compute-matched or wall-clock-matched early-stopping comparison is given.
[Reviewer-identified] The strongest empirical controls are negative: Adam sometimes wins, explicit reweighting can beat Muon, and full-matrix Shampoo does not always beat Adam.
[Reviewer-identified] The nonlinear logit-spectrum and token-frequency diagnostics are not the population data principal components defined in the proof.
[Reviewer-identified] The pinned PDF provides no author code or immutable experiment artifact, so the extensive sweep and figure results could not be independently replayed.
failure_modes: Fixed-step SpecGD can cycle around a component optimum whenever the target singular value is not divisible by the step size.

If weak spectral directions are noise, spurious features, or irrelevant tail structure rather than useful minority concepts, equal-rate learning can reduce generalization; later direct work documents such simplicity-bias failures.
When class means are correlated, have unequal norms, or covariance is anisotropic, spectral dominance need not correspond to class frequency and the theorem's basis decoupling fails.
Muon can lose to Adam when fine-tuning a pretrained representation or when Adam's elementwise adaptivity already handles imbalance.
Approximate Newton-Schulz orthogonalization, momentum, grafting, rectangular layers, and vector-parameter handling can move practical updates far from SpecGD.
Without a validation set, optimizer-specific test-set hyperparameter selection can overstate minority or worst-group gains.
Rare-token accuracy can reflect lexical/contextual difficulty rather than balanced spectral learning, especially in a 500-story sample.
For balanced or mildly imbalanced data, the benefit can vanish; reusing hyperparameters selected at severe imbalance obscures that crossover.
Uniformly amplifying all singular modes can fit rare noise earlier and remove the useful simplicity bias of SGD.
Early epoch advantages may disappear or reverse when compared at equal FLOPs or wall-clock time rather than equal update count.
reusable_insights: Optimizer comparisons can be made mechanistically interpretable by constructing data whose semantic groups align with known moment eigendirections.
A normalized matrix step can equalize coordinate speed while leaving component-specific stopping times; these are distinct properties.
Minority and worst-group metrics are more diagnostic than average accuracy when testing whether an optimizer learns weak components early.
Explicit reweighting is an essential control for claims that an optimizer obtains balancing 'for free.'
Moving from an ideal polar update to Muon requires separately auditing momentum, orthogonalization error, grafting, and non-matrix parameter updates.
A discrete normalized-gradient theorem must account for overshoot, step decay, clipping, or convergence to a neighborhood rather than importing a continuous-time saturation rule.
open_questions: Can a correct discrete SpecGD theorem quantify the oscillation neighborhood or establish convergence under decaying/clipped steps?
Which measurable finite-sample alignment condition can replace exact joint diagonalizability while preserving a minority-risk advantage?
Does equal-rate learning improve calibrated worst-group risk at matched FLOPs, wall time, and validation-selected hyperparameters?
When does removal of SGD's simplicity bias help minority signal rather than accelerate rare noise or spurious structure?
Can per-model logit or representation components be linked formally to class/group semantics in nonlinear networks?
Do the results persist with standard small-batch recipes, modern augmentation, weight decay, and large-scale language pretraining?
Which part of practical Muon matters most: polar normalization, momentum, Adam-updated vectors, or the Newton-Schulz approximation?
Can a causal spectral intervention that selectively suppresses weak modes reproduce or remove the reported generalization gain?

competitive_landscape.title: Heavy-Tailed Class Imbalance and Why Adam Outperforms Gradient Descent on Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: This earlier work already uses heavy-tailed imbalance to explain Adam's advantage over gradient descent. The target supplies an equal-singular-rate SpecGD account and minority-loss bounds, but Adam's strong target-paper results show the spectral account is not the only successful imbalance mechanism.

competitive_landscape.title: Muon Outperforms Adam in Tail-End Associative Memory Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: This paper directly studies Muon versus Adam on rare tail associations before the target's first submission. The target adds closed-form population trajectories and broader vision/group-imbalance plots, but it is not the first empirical claim that Muon improves tail learning.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Bias of Spectral Descent and Muon on Multiclass Separable Data
competitive_landscape.difference: This exact-current work characterizes spectral descent/Muon in multiclass separable classification and terminal max-margin bias. The target's narrower novelty is transient component learning and early population risk under imbalance rather than the optimizer's canonical form or implicit-bias framework.

competitive_landscape.title: Training Deep Learning Models with Norm-Constrained LMOs
competitive_landscape.difference: This work formalizes Muon-like updates as norm-constrained linear-minimization oracles and studies optimization. The target reuses the spectral-norm steepest-descent reduction but contributes an imbalance-specific generalization model.

competitive_landscape.title: Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers and Where to Find Them
competitive_landscape.difference: This benchmark treats tuning, recipes, and compute as first-class optimizer variables. The target offers more mechanism-specific imbalance analysis but lacks comparable compute matching and often selects from endpoint test curves.

competitive_landscape.title: Isotropic Curvature Model for Understanding Deep Learning Optimization: Is Gradient Orthogonalization Optimal?
competitive_landscape.difference: This paper identifies regimes where exact gradient orthogonalization is not optimal. It is negative evidence against treating equalized singular updates as universally beneficial and complements the target's own Adam and pretrained-fine-tuning failures.

competitive_landscape.title: Preconditioning Benefits of Spectral Orthogonalization in Muon
competitive_landscape.difference: This work derives benefits from low-rank gradients and structured Hessians rather than class-prior-aligned moment components. It broadens the possible Muon mechanism and makes the target's imbalance story one sufficient model rather than a general explanation.

competitive_landscape.title: To Use or not to Use Muon: How Simplicity Bias in Optimizers Matters
competitive_landscape.difference: This paper directly argues that Muon's simultaneous learning removes SGD's useful simplicity bias and gives cases where Muon fits spurious features or misses shared structure. It is the clearest current counterexample to interpreting balanced component speed as context-free generalization benefit.

competitive_landscape.title: Muon in Vision Transformers: Optimizer-Recipe Interactions and Gradient Spectra
competitive_landscape.difference: This work finds long-tail gains but shows they depend strongly on augmentation and optimizer recipe, with distinct spectral behavior across attention and MLP blocks. It supplies the controlled recipe interaction missing from the target's large-batch and unequal-regularization comparisons.

competitive_landscape.title: The Spectral Dynamics and Noise Geometry of Muon
competitive_landscape.difference: This paper emphasizes flat-spectrum implicit bias and batch-noise geometry and reports optimizer-ranking reversals across language and vision. Those reversals caution against extrapolating the target's population component-speed mechanism across domains and recipes.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards Understanding the Power and Limits of the Muon Optimizer: A River-Valley Perspective
competitive_landscape.difference: The river-valley analysis predicts fast early progress but late fixed-step overshoot and benefits from switching to AdamW. Its phase dependence is consistent with the target's transient gains but contradicts a blanket convergence/generalization interpretation.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first concrete generalization setting for spectrum-aware optimizers: exact SpecGD/GD trajectories show equal-rate component learning, early minority and balanced-risk gains that survive normalization of GD, depth amplification, and corresponding behavior across imbalanced vision and language tasks.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Sections 3.2-3.3 derive population GF/SpecGF loss gaps and deep-linear saturation times; Sections 2 and 4 plus Appendices C-D report synthetic, group-, class-, token-, and domain-imbalance experiments.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is an imbalance-specific continuous-time risk analysis that combines the established spectral steepest-descent update with a class-prior-aligned jointly diagonalizable model, plus a broad hypothesis-generating empirical panel. SpecGD/Muon, terminal implicit bias, imbalance-based Adam mechanisms, and rare-tail Muon gains all predate it. The exact discrete Proposition 1 is wrong without a terminal-step rule, and later work shows equalizing components can amplify spurious structure. The contribution should therefore be framed as one sufficient early-transient mechanism under strong alignment, not a general explanation of Muon generalization.

reviewer_notes: Primary pass used the exact current arXiv v3 submitted 2025-12-12 18:45:29 UTC. The official v3 URL reproduced the indexed 36-page PDF hash exactly, and the indexed text has all 36 pages with no missing-text pages. The paper was subsequently published at ICLR 2026 under OpenReview forum YzjS4jcfmS, but this record is intentionally pinned to the corpus's arXiv v3 bytes. All main text, proofs B.1-B.6, synthetic checks, experimental details D.1-D.10, related work, and limitations were read. High confidence attaches to the continuous-time algebraic mechanism conditional on its assumptions and to the discrete overshoot counterexample; lower confidence attaches to figure-only empirical magnitudes because the pinned paper supplies no author code URL, most results lack numerical tables/error bars, and several selection splits are ambiguous.
